title: The WMO Says This Could Be the Strongest El Niño on Record. India's Food Supply Is in the Path.
excerpt: An 80 per cent probability of El Niño by August, 90 per cent through November, and sea surface temperatures 6°C above average. The monsoon is already late.
body:
The World Meteorological Organisation issued its most definitive alert yet on Tuesday: there is an 80 per cent chance that El Niño conditions will develop between June and August 2026, and a 90 per cent chance they will persist through at least November. The WMO said this could become the strongest El Niño on record.

The announcement, timed for World Environment Day, carries more weight than a routine climate update. El Niño is not new. What makes 2026 different is the baseline it starts from. Global temperatures have already been pushed up roughly 1.3 degrees Celsius above pre-industrial levels by greenhouse gas emissions. Layer a potentially record-breaking El Niño on top of that, and the combination threatens to produce extreme weather the world has not seen before.

What the data says

Sea surface temperatures in the tropical Pacific are running at 6 degrees Celsius above average — an extraordinary departure that is fuelling the forecast for a strong, possibly super-strong, event. The last major El Niño in 2023-24 was among the five strongest on record and played a role in making 2024 the warmest year ever measured. The one forming now could surpass it.

WMO Secretary-General Celeste Saulo put it plainly: "The footprint of an El Niño extends far beyond its origins in the Pacific Ocean, impacting agriculture, energy supplies, trade, water resources, supply chains and livelihoods across entire regions."

UN Secretary-General António Guterres echoed the urgency: "The world must treat it as the urgent climate warning it is."

India stands directly in the path

India's exposure is acute. The IMD has already downgraded its monsoon forecast to 90 per cent of the long-period average — the weakest in 11 years. Its probability models assign an 84 per cent combined chance that monsoon rainfall will be below normal or worse. The Monsoon Core Zone, which covers the heart of India's rainfed farming belt, is expected to receive below-normal rains.

The monsoon reached Kerala on June 4, three days late. That delay matters: late onset often correlates with uneven distribution, prolonged dry spells, and reduced total rainfall. The monsoon delivers nearly 70 per cent of the rainfall India needs to water farms and replenish aquifers and reservoirs.

But India is not the only country at risk. Across Asia, dry weather is already disrupting crop planting. Wheat prices have climbed about 20 per cent since January. Rice prices at major Southeast Asian export hubs are up roughly 15 per cent in the past month alone. From Thailand's rice fields to Indonesia's palm oil plantations to Australia's eastern wheat belt, farmers are reducing plantings and bracing for worse.

The fertiliser squeeze makes everything harder

El Niño alone would be manageable if farmers could throw inputs at the problem. They cannot. The Iran war has effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz, choking off a major artery for global fertiliser trade. Nitrogen and phosphate prices have spiked. Diesel is expensive. Farmers in India, Southeast Asia and Africa face a choice between paying more for inputs they may not recoup, or planting less and accepting lower yields.

This is what the FAO calls a "systemic" agrifood shock: when multiple supply-side disruptions — weather, energy, conflict — hit simultaneously and compound each other. El Niño-driven dryness is a double blow for farmers already grappling with fertiliser and diesel shortages caused by the Iran war.

India's reservoir buffer — and its limits

India's Agriculture Ministry says reservoir storage remains 127 per cent of normal for this time of year, and CRISIL expects the reserves to cushion early-season sowing. Major agricultural states including Punjab, Haryana, Rajasthan, Uttar Pradesh, Gujarat, Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra and Karnataka are expected to see rainfall deficits, but irrigation penetration of 48 to 76 per cent in key regions should support crop establishment.

That is the good news. The bad news is that reservoirs buffer the planting phase, not the entire growing season. Productivity risks could emerge later due to moisture stress and tighter fertiliser availability. If the monsoon underperforms through July and August, no amount of stored water can replace the rainfall that 70 per cent of India's farmland depends on.

What this means for the diaspora

For NRIs, the El Niño warning matters on three levels. It means higher food prices in India, which erodes the purchasing power of remittances. It means potential export bans on rice and wheat, which India has used before and would use again if domestic stocks tighten. And it means a harder macroeconomic environment: food inflation forces the RBI into a corner, complicating rate decisions at a time when the rupee is already under siege.

Agriculture Minister Shivraj Singh Chouhan said the government is prioritising area-specific and crop-specific strategies, including timely advice for farmers, seed distribution, alternative crop options, delayed sowing plans and the promotion of drought-resistant varieties. Whether those measures are enough will depend on whether the monsoon delivers — or whether the strongest El Niño on record takes it away.
